routes.description: Establish that God concepts and religions are human cultural products by tracing their historical revision and cultural evolution, showing that bottom-up natural processes can explain complexity, consciousness, and morality, and challenging creator inferences from cosmology and fine-tuning.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if cultural evolution explains the formation and alteration of God concepts, naturalistic accounts remain viable for the phenomena assigned to God, and the proposed creator adds no necessary or intelligible explanatory step.

motionBridge.description: Connect the human formation and evolution of God concepts, together with adequate natural alternatives, to the conclusion that God is a human invention rather than a required creator.

centralBridges.description: Show that religions and God concepts arise, change, diversify, and disappear through deliberate design and cumulative cultural evolution.
Show that bottom-up evolutionary, scientific, and cultural processes can account for design, consciousness, agency, morality, and social goods without divine direction.
Show that cosmic beginnings and fine-tuning do not warrant a creator inference because natural alternatives remain possible and a creator compounds the explanatory demand.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish that publicly testable and corrigible inquiry offers a sounder method for disputed existential claims than appeals insulated from possible error.
Show that religion's historical or social benefits can be preserved by secular societies and therefore do not establish a supernatural source.

routes.description: Establish rational support for a real divine creator through a cumulative case from the universe's beginning, fine-tuned and intelligible order, consciousness, freedom, and morality, while distinguishing the human formation of religious concepts from the independent reality they may describe.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cumulative theistic explanation remains a coherent account of the cosmos and human nature, naturalistic alternatives leave relevant explanatory gaps, and cultural mediation of God concepts does not entail that their referent was invented.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative explanatory case and the concept-referent distinction to the conclusion that belief in a real divine creator has rational support despite human cultural mediation.

centralBridges.description: Show that the universe's beginning calls for a cause beyond nature and explain why that cause need not fall under the causal conditions internal to nature.
Show that life-permitting constants and the rational intelligibility of nature are better accounted for by purposive divine intelligence than by speculative alternatives.
Show that consciousness, intentionality, freedom, rational agency, and disinterested morality resist exhaustive material or evolutionary reduction and fit a spiritual source.
Show that a concept's human and culturally variable formation does not determine whether it refers to an independently existing divine reality.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish that finite sensory access and the limits of verification warrant epistemic humility rather than excluding realities not directly observable.
Show that religion's continuing vitality and contribution to moral and intellectual traditions support taking its claims seriously rather than treating it as dispensable fabrication.

sections.title: Cultural Origins and the Concept-Referent Distinction
sections.rationale: This issue directly tests whether the historical evolution and deliberate or cumulative design of God concepts establishes human invention, or whether culturally formed concepts may still describe an independent reality.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and Creator Regress
sections.rationale: The inference from the universe's beginning to a cause beyond nature is a principal route to a creator and must be assessed alongside objections about explanatory regress and the intelligibility of supernatural causation.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Anthropic Alternatives, and Intelligibility
sections.rationale: Life-permitting constants and the mind's ability to comprehend natural law provide a major design argument, opposed by anthropic selection, multiple-universe possibilities, and concerns about explanatory parsimony.

sections.title: Consciousness, Freedom, and Naturalistic Explanation
sections.rationale: Whether subjective experience, intentionality, rational agency, and free choice can arise through material and evolutionary processes bears directly on the claimed need for a nonmaterial or divine source.

sections.title: Morality and Religion's Social Role
sections.rationale: The debate requires comparison between divine and human-developmental accounts of morality, together with the disputed question whether secular societies can preserve moral and civic achievements associated with religion.

sections.title: Epistemic Standards, Inquiry, and Human Limits
sections.rationale: Competing standards of verification, corrigibility, subjective knowledge, and epistemic humility determine what kind of support a divine claim requires and whether its resistance to direct testing counts against it.
